summary: A 1975 official change to the Host-Host Protocol that clears up an ambiguity about the ERR command. It changes the documents NIC 8246 and NIC 7104.

plainLanguage.summary: A rule about an error message was unclear. This note fixes the wording so everyone follows it the same way.

subtitle: Clarification of the ERR command error codes.

tldr.problem: The Host-Host Protocol's ERR (Error) command with code 5 was ambiguous: it applied to two different error cases with different data formats, making it impossible to reliably distinguish them.
tldr.mechanism: The change assigns different error codes to the two cases: code 5 for a request on a non-open socket, and code 6 for a message on an unknown link. A new code 7 is added for invalid host headers.
tldr.outcome: The protocol becomes unambiguous. An NCP receiving an ERR command can now reliably interpret the contents of the data field by looking at the error code.

today: RFC 695 is an official protocol correction issued in July 1975 to clarify the ARPANET Host-Host Protocol. It remains a record of how protocol ambiguities were identified and resolved in the early ARPANET.

sections.title: The Ambiguity
sections.content:
The Host-Host Protocol specified an ERR (Error) command with error code 5 to mean "socket (link) not connected". However, this code applied to two distinct error cases: when a control command other than STR or RTS referred to a socket that was neither fully open nor fully closed, and when a non-control message arrived over a link not being used for a connection.

The two cases have fundamentally different data formats. In the first case, the data field contains a host-host command. In the second case, it contains a message header. There was no reliable way for an NCP receiving the ERR command to distinguish between the two cases by examining the data field, and no way for a human reviewing an error log to interpret the error correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: One error code meant two different things depending on the context, and there was no way to tell which was which when you saw the error.

sections.title: The Fix
sections.content:
The protocol change assigns separate error codes to each case and adds one more.

Error code 5: Request on a non-open socket. Issued when a request other than STR (Start) or RTS (Restart) is made for a socket that is not party to a fully established connection (perhaps because only one RFC has been sent, not yet opening, or only one CLS has been sent, not yet closing). The data field contains the erroneous command, with zeros as fill.

Error code 6: Message on an unknown link. Issued when a message arrives over a user link that is not currently being used for any connection. The data field contains the message header and the first eight bits of text, if present, or zeros.

Error code 7: Invalid host header. Issued when a message over the control link or a valid user link has a host header with invalid format, such as non-zero M1 or M2 fields, invalid byte size, or declared length exceeding actual length. The data field is the message header padded with eight zero bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Now each error code means exactly one thing. You can read the code number and know what went wrong.

sections.title: Improvement
sections.content: This change makes the protocol unambiguous and allows full use of the ERR command for debugging and troubleshooting. An NCP implementation can now reliably interpret error codes and a network troubleshooter can read error logs with confidence that the data field is in the expected format.
sections.plainLanguage: This makes the protocol clearer and easier for programmers to get right, and easier for people to understand when something goes wrong.
